text: Harlow Creek Logistics is a fictional mid-size logistics company with three product teams -- Dispatch, Fleet Analytics, and Customer Portal -- plus one central Platform team moving their first production workloads to Azure. This lesson turns the landing zone and network ideas from earlier chapters into one concrete design for that company.

Subscription boundaries get set by blast radius, not the org chart, so three product teams and one platform team becomes eight subscriptions, not four -- one production and one non-production subscription per product team, plus three platform subscriptions split by function: connectivity, identity, and management. The management group hierarchy mirrors that split, with every product team nested under mg-landing-zones so governance applies once and inherits everywhere.

The hub lives in its own subscription in East US 2, holding only shared services -- an Azure Firewall subnet, a gateway subnet for VPN or ExpressRoute, and a shared-services subnet for DNS. Each product team gets its own spoke VNet per environment, sized as a /20, and every spoke peers directly to the hub and never to another spoke, so cross-team traffic gets inspected at the firewall instead of flowing unmonitored.

Peering alone doesn't force traffic through the hub -- that takes an explicit user-defined route on every spoke subnet, sending all outbound traffic to the firewall's private IP as its next hop. Without that route, a virtual machine would reach the internet directly, completely bypassing the firewall the design just spent two steps building.

Governance guardrails get written as Azure Policy assigned at the management group level, not documented in a wiki nobody reads: deny public IPs on NICs, require cost-center and environment tags, restrict allowed regions, and require an NSG on every subnet. The allowed-locations policy is deliberately assigned one level higher than the others, so it constrains Platform's own subscriptions too, not just the product teams'.

Lesson 29 turned a landing zone and network from an idea into eight subscriptions, a management group hierarchy, real CIDR blocks, and four policy assignments. Lesson 30 writes down why each of those decisions was made, as real ADRs, and builds a disaster recovery plan with concrete RTO and RPO targets on top of this same design.
